first_comment: Bonus: Rwanda's Akagera park received 70 rhinos in one go, flown and driven about 3,400 km. Its white rhino herd is now just over 100. Which country would you visit to see them? 🦏

stories.headline: 745 rhinos moved from a farm into 19 wild parks
stories.summary: African Parks' Rhino Rewild has moved 745 southern white rhinos into 19 protected areas in 4 countries in 3 years. 89 calves have been born, though 61 rhinos died along the way.
stories.why: Spreading rhinos across many parks protects them from disease and poaching.

stories.headline: Gas-only cars dip below half of new car sales, a 1st
stories.summary: Gasoline-only cars made up 49% of global new car sales in early 2026, down from 73% in 2021. Electric cars took 17% and hybrids 18%.
stories.why: Electric and hybrid sales keep growing as gas-only sales fall.

stories.headline: A refugee teacher started a school in a camp with none
stories.summary: Isa fled war in Sudan and found no classrooms at a South Sudan settlement. He opened a school called "the future". Today more than 442 refugee children study across the camp's schools.
stories.why: Refugee and local kids now learn side by side.

stories.stat_label: of Antarctic ice turned into a telescope
stories.headline: A telescope made of Antarctic ice wins the physics Nobel
stories.summary: Francis Halzen won for leading IceCube, which uses thousands of light sensors frozen into a cubic kilometre of ice to catch 'ghost particles' from distant galaxies.
stories.why: Neutrinos reveal places in the universe ordinary telescopes can't see.

fun_fact: Halzen first pitched catching neutrinos in South Pole ice in 1988.
